introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 3 (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours fifteen minutes.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer ALL the THREE QUESTIONS. Question ONE carries thirty-four marks and the rest carry thirty-three marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed. Materials required: Topographic map, Photos, Graph Paper and outline map (where relevant).

**SECTION C - FIELDWORK AND PROJECT-BASED LEARNING**

**EITHER**

3. Based on an investigative fieldwork which you have carried out either in Physical or Human Geography, choose one of the following topics;

(EITHER part: sub-questions E1 to E8 below, TOTAL = 33 marks.)

**OR**

For any one Project-based study you have carried out on a topic drawn from one of the syllabus areas:

questions.enonce_markdown: EITHER i) Locate the area where your fieldwork was carried out. **(8 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**How to use this model answer.** The questions ask about the candidate's OWN fieldwork, so no single answer exists. The model below is written for the topic **Stream characteristics** (a study of one stream in Cameroon). All names and numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE: replace them by your own. The same plan works for the other topics (vegetation, soil, sphere of influence, land uses, CBD).

**Location (8 marks).** Give the answer in two parts.
1. *Written location (about 3 marks):* name of the stream (Stream X), the nearest town or village, the Division and Region, its position in relation to a well-known feature (road, school, main river), the approximate latitude and longitude or the grid reference on the topographic map, and the length of the stretch studied (for example 600 m from the upstream site to the downstream site).
2. *Sketch map (about 5 marks):* a neat map with a frame, title, north arrow, scale and key, showing the stream and its direction of flow, the sampling sites (Site 1 to Site 5 spaced at equal intervals), the nearby road or village, the relief (hills, valley) and the land use around (farmland, forest, houses). An inset map of Cameroon showing the Region gives extra credit.

questions.enonce_markdown: ii) State your objective and hypothesis for carrying out the field work. **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Objective (2 marks).** To find out how the characteristics of Stream X (channel width, depth, velocity and discharge) change along its course from the upstream site to the downstream site.

**Hypothesis (2 marks).** H1: channel width, depth, velocity and discharge increase downstream. A null hypothesis can also be stated: H0: there is no significant change in these characteristics downstream. A good hypothesis is short, testable with measurements, and linked to the objective.

questions.enonce_markdown: iii) What materials or tools did you use in carrying out the fieldwork? **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
List the tools and their uses (about eight tools, half a mark each, maximum 4 marks):
- Measuring tape (30 m) and ranging poles: to measure channel width and the distance between sites.
- Metre rule or graduated stick: to measure the depth of water at regular intervals across the channel.
- Float (an orange or a cork), stopwatch: to measure the speed of flow over a measured distance.
- Clinometer or abney level: to measure the gradient of the stream bed or banks.
- Pebbles/stones and a ruler (or callipers): to measure bed-load size and shape.
- Thermometer and pH paper: to record water temperature and quality.
- Field notebook, pencil, recording sheets, clipboard: to record data.
- Camera and GPS (or topographic map and compass): to record the sites and photograph them.
- Safety materials: boots and a first-aid kit.

questions.enonce_markdown: iv) How were the tools or materials used to obtain the data for the investigation? **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
Describe the method for each tool, in the order of the work (about eight points).
1. *Sampling:* five sites were chosen along the stream at equal intervals (systematic sampling), from upstream to downstream, so that the change along the course could be compared.
2. *Width:* at each site a tape was stretched across the channel from bank to bank (water's edge) and the width read in metres.
3. *Depth:* with the metre rule, the depth was measured at equal intervals (for example every 0.5 m) across the channel and the average depth calculated.
4. *Velocity:* a float was dropped upstream of a marked 10 m reach; the time taken to travel the 10 m was measured with the stopwatch, repeated three times and averaged: velocity = distance / time.
5. *Gradient and bed-load:* the clinometer was used to read the slope of the stream bed over a 10 m reach; 10 stones were picked at random from the bed and their longest axis measured with a ruler.
6. *Recording:* every reading was written in a table prepared beforehand, and each site was photographed and described.
(Describing at least four methods clearly earns the 4 marks.)

questions.enonce_markdown: v) How was your data processed and presented? **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Processing (2 marks).** The raw measurements were entered in a table site by site; the mean depth, the cross-sectional area (width x mean depth) and the discharge (Q = cross-sectional area x velocity, in m3/s) were calculated for each site; the mean and range of each characteristic were found.

**Presentation (3 marks, any three methods, with a reason).**
- Tables of the raw and calculated data (clear and compact).
- Line graphs of width, depth, velocity and discharge against distance downstream (to show the trend).
- Bar graphs of the average pebble size at each site.
- Cross-sectional profiles of the channel at the sites (to compare channel shapes).
- A sketch map of the stream with the sites and with proportional symbols for discharge.
- Photographs with annotations.
- Statistical tests (for example Spearman's rank correlation between the distance from the source and the pebble size) to check whether the trend is significant.

questions.enonce_markdown: vi) How did your findings relate to your hypothesis? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
State the main result, compare it with the hypothesis, and say whether it is accepted or rejected.

*Model (illustrative values).* Channel width rose from 1.8 m at Site 1 to 4.6 m at Site 5, mean depth from 0.12 m to 0.35 m, velocity from 0.20 m/s to 0.45 m/s, and discharge from about 0.04 m3/s to about 0.7 m3/s. These findings agree with the hypothesis, which is therefore **accepted** for the study stretch: the width, depth, velocity and discharge increase downstream. If one site differed (for example a velocity lower at a wide shallow site with boulders), say so and explain it with the local bed roughness: the hypothesis is accepted with a reservation.

Link the results to the geographical processes.
- The discharge increases downstream because more tributaries and more run-off and groundwater join the stream, so the cross-sectional area and the volume of water increase.
- The channel widens and deepens because the greater volume and energy of water erode the banks and bed (lateral and vertical erosion) downstream.
- The velocity increases despite the smaller gradient because the bigger channel is more efficient (less friction with the bed and banks relative to the volume of water) and the bed material is finer and smoother.

questions.enonce_markdown: viii) What lesson did you learn from carrying out the fieldwork? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
Give three lessons (1 mark each).
- Fieldwork gives first-hand, real data which supports the theories learnt in class (for example the Bradshaw model of a river's characteristics).
- Careful planning, repeated measurements and teamwork improve the accuracy and reliability of the data; human errors (timing, reading) can be reduced.
- Safety and respect for the environment and for the local people are essential (permission, avoiding flood days, no pollution).
- Limits of the study: the small sample, the single season and simple tools; a bigger sample over several seasons would give more reliable results.

questions.enonce_markdown: OR i) State the topic of the project and the duration of your study **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**How to use this model answer.** The questions ask about the candidate's OWN project-based study, so no single answer exists. The model below is written for an **illustrative** project, *a study of solid-waste disposal and its effects in one town neighbourhood*. Names, dates and numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE; replace them with your own. The same plan works for other projects of the syllabus areas (for example a soil-erosion study, a water-supply survey or a land-use survey).

**Topic and duration (3 marks).** Topic (2 marks): "The problems of solid-waste disposal in the X neighbourhood of Y town" (a clear, precise title that states the place and the issue). Duration (1 mark): for example, six weeks, from the first visit to the report, with the dates: planning (1 week), data collection (2 weeks), analysis and writing (3 weeks).

questions.enonce_markdown: ii) locate the area where the project was carried out. **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
Give a written location and a sketch map.
- *Written (about 2 marks):* name of the neighbourhood, town, Division and Region; distance and direction from the town centre or a known landmark; approximate coordinates or grid reference; the size of the study area.
- *Sketch map (about 3 marks):* frame, title, north arrow, scale and key, with the roads, the main buildings, the rubbish dumps or bins, the drainage channel or stream and the boundaries of the study area; an inset of Cameroon with the Region.

questions.enonce_markdown: iii) State the objective and possible outcome (hypothesis) **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Objectives (3 marks).** (1) To identify the sources and kinds of solid waste and how it is disposed of in the neighbourhood; (2) to find out the effects of poor disposal on the environment and on health; (3) to suggest solutions.

**Possible outcome / hypothesis (2 marks).** Most households have no regular waste collection, so much of the waste is dumped in open spaces and drains, which causes blocked drains, bad smell and a higher risk of flooding and disease. (State it so that it can be tested by the survey.)

questions.enonce_markdown: iv) Describe the problem you identified and state why it was necessary for the investigation **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The problem (3 marks).** Describe it with evidence: rubbish piled up at the roadside and in the drainage channel, burning of waste, irregular collection by the council, bad smell, flies and blocked drains in the rainy season (illustrative observations).

**Why the investigation was necessary (2 marks).** The problem affects the health and the comfort of the residents (cholera and malaria risks), pollutes water and soil, and increases the flooding of the neighbourhood; no precise data existed, so facts were needed to guide the council and the inhabitants.

questions.enonce_markdown: v) Describe the materials/equipment and methods used for the investigation **(7 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Materials/equipment (about 3 marks).** Questionnaire forms and clipboard, a notebook and pencil, a camera (or phone), a base map or sketch map of the area, a measuring tape (to measure the distance of dumps from houses), gloves and a mask (safety), a calculator; a hand GPS or a mobile phone to record the positions of the dumps.

**Methods (about 4 marks).**
1. Reconnaissance visit and permission from the neighbourhood chief and the council.
2. *Sampling:* a systematic (or stratified) sample of, say, 50 households in the area, so that every part of the neighbourhood was represented.
3. *Questionnaire and interviews:* questions on the quantity of waste, the means of disposal, the frequency of collection and the health problems; an interview of an official of the council's sanitation service.
4. *Observation and mapping:* all the dumps were located and described (size, content, distance from houses and drains) on a map; photographs were taken.
5. Data were collected in two weeks, at different hours, and checked each day.

questions.enonce_markdown: vi) How was the data analysed and what were the results. **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Analysis (about 3 marks).** The questionnaires were coded and tallied; the answers were converted into frequencies and percentages and presented in tables, bar charts and pie charts; the dumps were shown on a distribution map; photographs were annotated; the relation between the distance from a dump and the number of reported illnesses was checked, for example with a scatter graph or Spearman's rank correlation.

**Results (about 2 marks), illustrative.** For example: about 60 % of the households dispose of their waste in open spaces or drains; only a small share has a regular collection; most of the dumps are close to the drainage channel; households near dumps reported more cases of malaria and diarrhoea. The hypothesis was therefore confirmed. (Quote your own results.)

questions.enonce_markdown: vii) What can be done to solve the problem? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
Three measures (1 mark each).
- Organise a regular waste-collection service by the council (and private collectors), with enough bins and skips in good locations.
- Educate the residents (campaigns in schools, churches and markets) about sorting, reduction and not throwing waste into drains; apply fines to offenders.
- Recycle and compost (organic waste into manure, plastics into products) and create small jobs for the youth; build a controlled landfill away from houses and rivers; clean and maintain the drainage channels.
